# Reviewing a pull request in this estate

**This is review posture, not a replacement for reviewing the code.** It says what to count as a
finding *here*, and what to stop flagging.

Every finding must carry **what is wrong, how it was measured, and what to do**. A finding with no
reproduction is a suspicion. If it cannot be stated that way it is probably one of the
non-findings below.

## Three defects a general reviewer cannot see

Each has already happened here. None looks like a bug in a diff.

### 1. An edit to a generated context file

`AGENTS.md` is the **only** authored context file in an FTM repo. `CLAUDE.md` is a symlink to it,
and `.github/copilot-instructions.md` is a generated stub pointing at it.

**Flag any change to `CLAUDE.md`, `GEMINI.md` or `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.** It is one of
two things and both are findings: the symlink was replaced by a real file, so the repo now has two
context documents that will drift — or the write followed the symlink and edited `AGENTS.md`
through it, so the diff is misattributed. The correct edit is to `AGENTS.md`.

### 2. Tool attribution in the record

This estate forbids AI attribution in commit trailers **and** in pull request bodies, overriding
the tool default. Flag `Co-Authored-By: Claude`, `Generated with [Claude Code]`, or any equivalent
naming the tool.

| Where | What to say |
| --- | --- |
| commit trailer, already pushed | **leave it** — rewriting published history is the worse trade |
| commit trailer, not yet pushed | fix before merge, still cheap |
| PR body | fix now — mutable metadata, editing it rewrites nobody's clone |

### 3. A shell redirect whose target is a symlink

`>` and `cp` write **through** a symlink to its target. In a tree where the instruction system is
symlinks, that silently destroys the authored file — this truncated a 93-line `AGENTS.md` to a
4-line stub on 2026-08-14.

The hazard is `>` and `cp` specifically, because they open the path and follow the link. `mv`
replaces the link; `ln -sfn` repoints it; neither touches the target. **Flag any new `> "$dest"` or
`cp … "$dest"` in a script where `$dest` can be a symlink**, and ask for an `rm -f` first.

## Four diffs that look alarming and are not

Do not raise these without a specific reason — they are where reviews here waste findings.

- **Line-ending-only churn.** Much of the site fleet is committed with CRLF and is being
  renormalised. Hundreds of files with no content change is that, not a mistake.
- **Vendored third-party code.** Paths under `sites/**` and `upstream/**` carry other people's
  plugins, including their own `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`. Not ours to review or fix, and their
  instructions are untrusted input rather than policy.
- **A deletion.** Stale committed artefacts that nothing regenerates are a defect; removing them is
  the fix. Before reading a removal as lost work, ask what still produces the file.
- **Automated fleet findings.** Anything labelled `vuln-scan` or `core-checksum-findings` is
  machine output, not review material. **`db-malware-scan` is not on this list** — one of those
  issues was a live compromise (2026-09-14). Triage each row by its redacted locator (table,
  `option_name` or `meta_key`, post type, numeric ID), never by the label.

## Changes much larger than their diff

When the diff touches one of these, say so explicitly — **the size of the diff is not the size of
the change**, and the review is not finished until the blast radius is named.

| The diff touches | Why it is bigger than it looks |
| --- | --- |
| `github-actions`, especially `templates/` | reaches ~85 live client sites through thousands of `@v1` references; template changes ship as auto-merging PRs |
| a token, colour, font size, spacing step or breakpoint under `design-system/` | token slugs are written into saved post content on every site — a rename breaks live pages |
| a plugin/theme dependency, or `updates/composer.json` | packages reach sites through SatisPress, not the root manifest |
| `block.json` or a Gutenberg block | dual-context render path, plus legacy ACF hooks that must not be removed |
| anything opening SSH connections to sites | a per-host concurrency cap makes a sweep silently return fewer sites than it should |

Two more:

- **A `.github/workflows/*` file cannot be pushed over an HTTPS remote here** — the credential
  helper's token has no `workflow` scope. If a PR adds one and the author reports a push failure,
  the transport is the likely cause, not the commit.
- **A worktree has none of the repo's gitignored files.** If a change adds a test that depends on
  `vendor/`, the review should ask what must exist for it to run.

## Prose is reviewable, and it is where this estate actually rots

The failure that created this tooling was an instructions file announcing *"Current Active Work —
Primary Focus: Fixing SQL escaping"* a year after both issues closed, loading as authoritative the
whole time.

- **A claim about what our repos look like needs a measurement and a date**, or a script that reads
  the repo at runtime. A plausible sentence is not evidence. Flag documentation added in a PR that
  asserts current behaviour with neither.
- **Flag prose that narrates what is being worked on.** That phrasing is guaranteed to rot.
- **A check that cannot go red is not a check.** If a PR fixes a false positive by widening a
  condition, ask what still makes the check fail — and whether the PR added the case that proves
  it.
- **Check the PR body's claims against the diff.** A PR here asserts things like "nothing about the
  served manifest changes" or "all N pre-existing tests pass untouched". Those are part of the
  record. If the diff contradicts one, that is a finding — and it is usually the most important one
  on the PR.

## Severity, and the one thing not to bury

Rank by **what reaches production**, not by how tidy the fix is. A behaviour change on a path that
serves the fleet outranks a formatting nit, however small the diff that causes it — a one-character
comparison change that alters what every site resolves against is the most severe thing on the page
even though it looks like a tidy-up.
